resumen: This topic groups 621 papers on pain, fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome and other functional or somatic syndromes, with ME/CFS as one condition among several. Most papers study comorbidity, population epidemiology, psychosocial factors and central sensitization. More than half mention ME/CFS only in passing. The defining issue is whether these conditions form one shared spectrum or remain separate entities.
sintesis: The topic gathers 621 papers from 2010 to 2026 on chronic pain, fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), interstitial cystitis and other functional syndromes. The most frequent keywords are 'chronic fatigue syndrome' (358), 'fibromyalgia' (257) and 'irritable bowel syndrome' (123). The journals with the most papers are the Journal of Psychosomatic Research (26) and The Journal of Urology (23). The 80-paper sample mixes laboratory pain studies, population cohorts, reviews on classification and a few marginal hypotheses. ME/CFS is sometimes the object of study and sometimes a condition attached to another main diagnosis.

One line in the sample studies pain in ME/CFS with experimental measures. Pressure pain thresholds were lower in patients with CFS and fell after submaximal exercise [#20]. A narrative review concludes that generalized hyperalgesia supports central sensitization in CFS [#696], and another argues for treating pain as a specific symptom [#1147]. A second line comes from urology. The MAPP network and other interstitial cystitis studies describe how the condition coexists with IBS, fibromyalgia and CFS [#292, #1869, #3752]. Gastroenterology studies of IBS show the same pattern [#202, #5508].

Epidemiology and risk-factor studies rely on large cohorts. In the Danish DanFunD cohort, 16.3% of participants met criteria for at least one functional somatic syndrome, and CFS reached 8.6% [#3727]. In Lifelines, the three main diagnoses overlapped 45 times more than chance predicts [#5807]. A meta-analysis links psychological trauma to these syndromes (pooled odds ratio 2.7) [#1589]. Swedish and Dutch registry studies quantify the familial and genetic risk that ME/CFS, fibromyalgia, IBS and internalizing disorders share [#4824, #6095, #6923].

Output on the topic is steady. Papers per year range from 24 (2016) to 46 (2021), and 2026 has 28 with the year incomplete until October. Only 165 papers in the topic are central to ME/CFS and 99 are secondary. Another 349 (56%) mention it in passing, and 8 are uncertain or concern another concept. The topic talks to other topics more than chance predicts with cognitive behavioral therapy, PACE and patient experience (O/E 1.36), exercise, autonomic system and brain (1.25), and fatigue, sleep and stress (1.17). It talks less with XMRV retrovirus (0.39), immunity, mitochondria and biomarkers (0.66) and long COVID (0.76). Coupling with exercise and the autonomic system rises from 0.069 (2010-2012) to 0.473 (2024-2026). Coupling with cognitive behavioral therapy falls from 0.681 to 0.364, and with traditional Chinese medicine from 0.708 to 0.13.

Classification runs through the whole sample. Some papers group ME/CFS with fibromyalgia and IBS as functional or 'central sensitivity' syndromes [#2346, #5513, #6095]. Others treat it as its own entity with distinct features, for example in symptom patterns or genetic risk [#3660, #4824]. A psychiatric review acknowledges that classification is disputed and that patients and the medical establishment hold very different views [#3299]. Isolated hypotheses sit outside this axis. A hypermobility series in CFS [#4254, #5759] and a cranial venous obstruction model [#4506] offer ideas with little data. One author wrote all four papers on stealth adapted viruses, which have 10 citations at most [#3822, #4954].

lineas.texto: Several papers describe generalized hyperalgesia in ME/CFS and abnormal pain modulation during exercise [#696, #1147]. In one experimental study, 26 patients with CFS and pain had lower pressure thresholds than controls, and those thresholds fell after exercise while they rose in the other groups [#20]. Another study measured pain inhibition and postexertional malaise in 22 women with ME/CFS [#156], and a trial compared endogenous modulation in CFS with fibromyalgia, rheumatoid arthritis and controls [#1711]. An editorial notes that pain appears in the usual diagnostic criteria but has received little study [#3461].

lineas.titulo: Overlap with IBS, cystitis and pelvic pain
lineas.texto: In women with interstitial cystitis, IBS (38.6% vs 5.2%), fibromyalgia (17.7% vs 2.6%) and CFS (9.5% vs 1.7%) were more common than in controls [#292]. In the MAPP network, 38% of 424 participants with urological pelvic pain had another nonurological somatic syndrome [#1869], and a case-control study compared pelvic pain with other overlapping pain conditions [#3752]. In IBS, IL-1β and TNFα were higher in patients with extraintestinal comorbidities [#202]. Among 595 patients with ME/CFS, 76% had at least one overlapping pain condition [#5994].

The DanFunD cohort describes 9,656 Danish adults [#2817] and estimates that 16.3% meet criteria for at least one functional syndrome [#3727]. In Canada, 1.4% reported diagnosed CFS and 1.5% fibromyalgia [#2071]. In Lifelines, the three main diagnoses coincide far more than chance predicts [#5807], and all three conditions go with more mood and anxiety disorders [#2114]. Other papers analyze who receives a diagnostic label [#5834, #6766].

A meta-analysis of 71 studies links trauma to functional somatic syndromes, with a larger association for CFS than for IBS [#1589]. A review summarizes stress and HPA-axis findings in three of these syndromes [#598]. In Swedish registers, fibromyalgia shows a broader familial genetic risk profile than IBS and CFS [#4824]. In Lifelines, familiality ranged from 22% in IBS to 42% in ME/CFS [#6095], and a twin study puts heritability between 15% and 44% [#6923].

A review notes that some people with CFS may have unrecognized Ehlers-Danlos syndrome [#2823]. Among 63 patients with fibromyalgia or ME/CFS, 81% met criteria for hypermobility syndrome [#4254]. In the You + ME registry, a fraction of the 815 participants had hypermobility and more often reported Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and POTS [#5759]. One clinical group proposes that CFS relates to idiopathic intracranial hypertension and to cranial venous outflow obstruction, based on small series and a single case report [#1571, #1881, #4506, #5294].

Four papers by one author describe a virus derived from an African green monkey cytomegalovirus, repeatedly cultured from the blood of a person with CFS, which allegedly incorporated cellular and bacterial sequences [#3822, #4954]. The texts discuss its public health implications [#4926, #5205]. This is a marginal, little-cited line, with 1 to 10 citations per paper.

consensos.texto: ME/CFS, fibromyalgia and IBS occur in the same patients far more often than chance predicts. In Lifelines, the three diagnoses coincided 45 times more than expected [#5807], and in DanFunD their mutual overlaps also exceeded chance [#3727]. Their symptoms overlap widely [#3660].

In the sample, experimental studies indicate altered pain perception in ME/CFS. Pressure pain thresholds were lower than in controls [#20], and the central sensitization review reports generalized hyperalgesia [#696]. A neuroimaging review finds augmented sensory responses across several central sensitivity syndromes [#2346].

Mood and anxiety disorders are more frequent in these conditions than in people without them, although most patients do not have them. In a cohort of 94,516 participants, prevalence of these disorders was low (1.6% to 28.6%) [#2114]. In another study, psychiatric disorders were most common in fibromyalgia, followed by chronic pain and CFS [#6391].

Exposure to trauma associates with functional somatic syndromes. The meta-analysis estimates an odds ratio of 2.7 [#1589], and other papers examine childhood stressors and intimate partner violence [#1538, #3819].

Self-reported diagnosis identifies cases poorly against case definitions. Self-report of physician diagnosis missed 90% of controls who had CFS by case definition [#1186], and many people who meet criteria hold no diagnostic label [#6766, #5834].

debates.texto: Researchers disagree on whether ME/CFS is its own entity or part of a spectrum of functional syndromes. Some papers suggest shared pathophysiology [#4003] or a common multifactorial model [#2151], and the familial correlation between ME/CFS and fibromyalgia was +0.97 [#6095]. Others stress differences, such as pain that worsens the day after activity in 94% of fibromyalgia and 85% of CFS against 32% of IBS [#3660], or a distinct genetic profile for fibromyalgia [#4824]. A psychiatric review states that classification is disputed [#3299], and a hypermobility study raises the same question for fibromyalgia and ME/CFS [#4254].

Papers differ on whether the origin is psychological or biological. One review defends the evidence for central sensitization against a purely psychological explanation [#696], and another proposes inflammatory biological phenotypes for physio-somatic symptoms [#1485]. An umbrella review found that 90% of reviews addressed biological factors and 33% psychological ones [#5513]. Other papers highlight stress as a pathophysiological factor [#598].

The timing of psychopathology remains contested. Mental health problems preceded diagnoses of IBS, CFS and fibromyalgia in primary care [#6913], and a prior psychological disorder raised the risk of CFS (HR 2.08) after gastrointestinal infection [#2948]. Other papers describe psychopathology as a marker of severity within ME/CFS [#2073, #2804], and a longitudinal study compares which aspects of mental health predict these syndromes [#2016].

Papers weigh the clinical importance of hypermobility in ME/CFS differently. A study of 63 patients found that 81% met criteria for hypermobility syndrome and that hypermobility scores predicted symptom levels [#4254], and a review notes that up to 30-57% of patients with ME/CFS and related conditions have it [#5952]. Another review states that hypermobility does not appear clinically relevant for musculoskeletal pain in CFS [#1413]. The registry analysis asks whether it defines a subgroup [#5759].

lagunas.texto: Many papers use self-reported diagnoses, questionnaires or administrative codes instead of clinical assessment. Hospital codes give 0.42% CFS among patients with IBS [#5508], and self-reported diagnosis misses most cases [#1186]. Few papers in the sample apply standardized clinical assessment [#5454, #5834].

Experimental and clinical pain studies in ME/CFS have small samples and few replications. They include 26 patients with CFS [#20], 22 with ME/CFS [#156], 19 with CFS and fibromyalgia [#1711] and 29 in the lumbar puncture series [#1881]. The cranial venous hypothesis rests on series and isolated cases [#4506, #5294].

Mechanisms and causal direction remain unresolved. Neuroimaging finds no signature of its own, and the literature cannot say whether sensory augmentation is a cause, a predisposing factor or an epiphenomenon [#2346]. Methodological quality of the etiology reviews was low or critically low in 41% [#5513]. Cross-sectional designs limit causal inference about psychopathology [#5358, #6718].

Diagnostic criteria vary across studies and complicate comparison. Chronicity thresholds (three to six months) and interference requirements differ between the CFS, fibromyalgia and IBS criteria, and aligning them raised the overlap to 152 times [#5807]. Some samples come from self-help websites [#3660] or general practices [#4102], and only a few, such as the MCAM study, analyze ME/CFS as its own entity [#5994].

The sample comes mostly from Europe and North America. Few papers study specific populations, such as US veterans [#5454, #5840], a survey in Al-Baha [#6127] or people using opioids [#6461]. Replication in other countries and in patients with a strict ME/CFS diagnosis is missing.
